etymology: From English talk and stage. The phrase arose among American teenagers on Twitter and Snapchat in the mid-2010s (c. 2015–2017) for the period of texting, flirting, and spending time together before two people call themselves a couple, and it was standard TikTok vocabulary by about 2020 ("we’re just talking," "stuck in the talking stage"). It displaced older phrases like seeing someone and going steady; a grandparent’s nearest equivalent is courting, which had a destination the talking stage lacks.
biblical_def: In current slang the talking stage is the undefined season before dating: two people text every day, flirt, perhaps spend time together, but neither has said what this is, and either can drift away without a word. It can last weeks or months, run alongside other "talking stages," and end in ghosting rather than goodbye. The Christian observation: getting to know someone before marriage is wise, and Scripture is warm toward a man who seeks a wife, for "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing" (Pro 18:22). The trouble is not the talking; it is a stage with no exit. It lets hearts be stirred while no one is responsible for them, and the Song warns, "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). It trains young people to keep their options open and their words vague, when Christ said, "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). Rebekah was asked one plain question, "Wilt thou go with this man?" and gave one plain answer: "I will go" (Gen 24:58). Paul wants every believer to know how to keep himself "in sanctification and honour" (1Th 4:4), and honour includes not toying with another person’s affections. A father tells his son: if you are not ready to say what your intentions are, you are not ready to be messaging her every night; and if you are, say it, to her and to her father. He tells his daughter: a young man who will only "talk" for months has already told you how much he is willing to give.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Twitter / Snapchat c. 2015, TikTok-standard by 2020) for the undefined pre-dating season of texting and flirting — a season Scripture would fill with plain intentions, honour, and a yes that means yes.
webster_full: TALKING STAGE, n. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2015–present; American teen social media) The undefined period of texting, flirting, and spending time together before two people call themselves a couple. "We’re not dating, we’re in the talking stage."
Talking, v.i., in the same sense: "Are you two talking?" Stuck in the talking stage, a relationship that never becomes defined. Talking to several people at once is common and accepted in the slang.
A grandparent’s nearest words: courting, keeping company, going steady — each of which named a stage with an aim.

Webster (1828), root word talk: “TALK, verb intransitive tauk. 1. To converse familiarly; to speak, as in familiar discourse, when two or more persons interchange thoughts. I will buy with you, sell with you, talk with you; but I will not eat with you. In Aesop's time When all things talk'd, and talk'd in rhyme. I will come down and talk with thee. Numbers 11:17.”
Decode for parents: "we’re just talking" can mean hours of private messages a night with no one, including the two of them, accountable for where it is going.
scriptures: Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD.
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.
That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
corruption_summary: The talking stage keeps hearts engaged and intentions undeclared, so that affection can be stirred, shared, and dropped without anyone owning a word of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation has had a season between strangers and spouses; what is new is a season designed to commit to nothing. The talking stage lets a boy and a girl share their days, their secrets, and their late-night messages while either may say, at any moment, that it was never anything. It is often run with two or three others in parallel, and it often ends not with a conversation but with silence. The Song of Solomon counsels the opposite pace: "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7) — do not wake what you are not ready to keep.

Scripture’s courtships are short on ambiguity. Abraham’s servant states his errand before he eats; Rebekah answers, "I will go" (Gen 24:58); Boaz settles the matter at the gate before witnesses the same day. Christ’s rule for speech, "Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37), binds the heart as much as the marketplace. Teach your children that getting to know someone is good and that leaving someone guessing is unkind; a young man who means it will say so, and a family that loves its daughter will ask him to.
roots_summary: Middle English talken (to converse) + stage (a step or period) → mid-2010s teen social media: talking, the pre-dating phase → c. 2020 TikTok: the talking stage.
roots_lines: Middle English talken — to converse, related to tale and tell
Old French estage — a standing place, a floor; English stage, a step in a process
2000s: talking to someone, a soft phrase for early romantic interest
c. 2015–2017 Twitter and Snapchat: the talking stage
c. 2020 TikTok: the stage nobody leaves, and the ghosting that ends it
usage: "We’ve been in the talking stage since August and he still hasn’t asked me out."
Let your yea be yea, in courtship too (Mat 5:37).
Do not wake a love you are not ready to keep (Son 2:7).

etymology: Borrowed from marketing and tech jargon, where a soft launch is a quiet trial release and a hard launch the full public one. On Instagram and TikTok c. 2020–2022 the pair moved into dating: a soft launch hints at a new partner (a second coffee cup, a hand in the frame, a shoulder), and a hard launch posts his or her face and name — the relationship made public, usually in a carousel of photos. The term is now used of anything revealed outright ("hard-launching my new job").
biblical_def: In current slang to hard launch a relationship is to post it publicly for the first time — face, name, a caption — after weeks or months of hints. It is the reveal after the tease, and it is often treated as the moment a relationship becomes real. The Christian observation: Scripture agrees that a covenant should be public. Boaz did not take Ruth in secret; he sat at the city gate before the elders and said, "ye are witnesses this day" (Rut 4:10). "Marriage is honourable in all" (Heb 13:4), and a candle is not lit to be put "under a bushel, but on a candlestick" (Mat 5:15). So the instinct behind the hard launch has something right in it: a real bond wants witnesses. But the slang has the order and the audience wrong. The witnesses Scripture wants are parents, elders, and the church, not followers; and the publicity it honours is the publicity of a vow, not of a photo carousel that can be deleted when the relationship ends. The launch also invites a contest: a couple announced for applause is a couple performing, and "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2). Christ will one day make His own bride public before heaven and earth, and that announcement will never be taken down: "the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready" (Rev 19:7). A father tells his daughter: the first people who should know about a young man are under this roof, not on your feed. He tells his son: if you are proud of her, tell her father before you tell the internet.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Instagram / TikTok c. 2020–present, from marketing jargon) for revealing a relationship outright online — a right instinct for public witness aimed at the wrong audience.
webster_full: HARD LAUNCH, n. / v.t. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; from marketing jargon) The open, unmistakable public reveal of a romantic relationship online, with the partner’s face and name. "She finally hard launched him."
Contrasted with soft launch, a hinted reveal (a hand, a second plate, a shoulder in frame). Extended to any outright announcement: "hard-launching my new haircut."
Older sense: in business, the full public release of a product or service after a trial period.

Webster (1828), root word announce: “ANNOUNCE, verb transitive announs'. […] 1. To publish; to proclaim; to give notice, or first notice; as, the birth of Christ was announced by an angel. 2. To pronounce; to declare by judicial sentence.”
Decode for parents: for your teen a relationship can feel unofficial until it is posted and official the moment it is — which means the feed, not the family, is holding the ceremony.
scriptures: Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place: ye are witnesses this day.
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.
corruption_summary: The hard launch keeps the old truth that love wants witnesses but hands the witnessing to followers, making a photo the ceremony and applause the vow.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture’s weddings are public on purpose. Boaz gathers ten elders at the gate and declares his intent aloud, "ye are witnesses this day" (Rut 4:10); Cana has a feast and guests; the covenant is spoken before God and men because the community is to hold the couple to it. The hard launch borrows that instinct and empties it. The witnesses are strangers, the declaration costs nothing, and the archive can be quietly scrubbed when the thing ends — which, among teenagers, it usually does.

There is a second snare in the word: a launch is a performance, and performers watch the numbers. A relationship announced for likes becomes one more thing to be ranked, and "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2). Point your children to the launch that matters. The marriage of the Lamb will be announced in heaven, "and his wife hath made herself ready" (Rev 19:7) — a bride made public by her Bridegroom, never to be deleted. Let a courtship be known first to the family and the church; the feed can hear about it at the wedding.
roots_summary: Late Latin lanceare (to wield a lance) → English launch, to set a ship afloat → marketing soft / hard launch → c. 2020 Instagram: revealing a partner outright.
roots_lines: Late Latin lanceare — to wield a lance; Old North French lancher → English launch, to hurl, then to set a ship on the water
20th c.: to launch a product, a campaign, a rocket
Business jargon: soft launch (quiet trial) and hard launch (full release)
c. 2020–2022 Instagram and TikTok: soft-launching and hard-launching a partner
Now: any outright public reveal
usage: "Three months of soft launches and he finally hard launched her on his story."
Boaz launched at the gate, before elders and witnesses (Rut 4:10).
Let another praise your love, not your own caption (Pro 27:2).

etymology: A red flag has signalled danger, defiance, or battle for centuries — at sea, on 19th-century railways, at firing ranges and beaches — and the figurative red flag, a warning sign, was ordinary 20th-century English (auditors and bankers speak of "red flags" in the books). Gen Z made it a dating category: on Twitter and TikTok c. 2020–2021 the red-flag emoji became shorthand for a trait that marks someone as a bad partner, and "red flags in a guy" and "red flags in a girl" lists ran by the thousand.
biblical_def: In current slang a red flag is a warning sign in a person, especially a prospective boyfriend or girlfriend: he is rude to waiters, she lies easily, he has no friends who have known him longer than a year. Teens post lists of them and drop the emoji under a friend’s photo as a joke. The Christian observation: this is one of the more biblical things the slang does. Proverbs is a book of red flags. "Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul" (Pro 22:24–25). Christ Himself taught discernment by fruit: "Ye shall know them by their fruits" (Mat 7:16), and Paul warns Timothy of men "Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away" (2Ti 3:5). "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15). The slang errs in two places. It often flags trivia (bad taste in music) while waving through real sin (a boy who mocks his mother), and it almost never turns the flag around. Christ does: "why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" (Mat 7:3). A father tells his daughter: learn your red flags from Proverbs, not from TikTok, and believe them the first time. He tells his son: before you list hers, ask the Lord to show you yours.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (TikTok / Twitter c. 2020–present, from the old danger signal) for a warning sign in a person — the discernment by fruit that Proverbs teaches, best applied first to oneself.
webster_full: RED FLAG, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; from the danger signal) A trait or behaviour that warns a person may be a poor friend or partner. "He’s rude to his mom. Red flag."
Often posted as the red-flag emoji alone, or in lists ("red flags in a guy"). Used jokingly of trivial preferences: "You put ketchup on that? Red flag."
Older senses: a signal of danger or of battle at sea and on railways; a revolutionary banner; in business and law, a sign that something in the record needs checking.
Webster (1828), root word warning: “WARNING, participle present tense Cautioning against danger; admonishing; giving notice to; summoning to meet or appear.”
Decode for parents: your teen already has a vocabulary for discernment; give it a better list, and teach him to read it in the mirror.
scriptures: Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go:
Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.
Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
corruption_summary: Red flag recovers a little of Proverbs’ discernment but spends it on trivia and on other people, rarely on real sin and almost never on oneself.
corruption_paragraphs: There is wisdom in the word. Scripture tells the young to watch for warning signs in companions: the angry man (Pro 22:24), the flatterer, the talebearer, the son who mocks his father. A girl who learns to notice how a boy speaks to his mother has learned something Proverbs wanted her to learn. "The prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15). In a generation told never to judge, a red flag is a quiet admission that character can be read.

But the slang’s list is shaped by the feed, not by the fear of the Lord. It flags his height or her taste in films and ignores the boy who never darkens a church door and the girl who lies to her parents. And it points one way: outward. Christ teaches discernment and self-examination in the same breath, the beam before the mote (Mat 7:3). Teach your children to read fruit (Mat 7:16), to take the real warnings seriously, and to ask what flags others are seeing in them — then to bring those to the cross rather than to the comments.
roots_summary: Old English read (red) + flag (a banner) → danger and battle signals at sea and on railways → 20th-c. figurative warning sign → c. 2020 TikTok: a warning trait in a partner.
roots_lines: Old English read — red, the colour of blood and fire
16th c. English flag — a banner or ensign, origin uncertain
17th–19th c.: red flag hoisted for battle at sea, for danger on railways and firing ranges
20th c.: figurative red flag in business and law — a sign that needs checking
c. 2020–2021 TikTok and Twitter: the red-flag emoji and lists of warning traits in a partner
usage: "He doesn’t talk to any of his old friends? That’s a red flag."
Proverbs keeps the real list: the angry man first among them (Pro 22:24).
Check for the beam before you flag the mote (Mat 7:3).

etymology: Coined as the opposite of red flag on Twitter and TikTok c. 2020–2021. The green flag already meant "go" or "all clear" in railway signalling and in motor racing, where it starts or restarts a race. In the slang a green flag is a sign that a person is kind, trustworthy, and worth pursuing, often posted with a green emoji.
biblical_def: In current slang a green flag is a good sign in a person: he texts back when he says he will, she is kind to her little brother, he respects your parents, she says sorry without being made to. It is the slang’s attempt at a list of virtues. The Christian observation: Scripture is full of green flags, and it gives them a name — fruit. "Every good tree bringeth forth good fruit" (Mat 7:17), and the fruit is listed: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance" (Gal 5:22–23). Paul’s list of things to think on is a green-flag list for a whole life: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure" (Php 4:8). The slang is right to look for character rather than looks alone, for "the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). But its green flags tend to be manners and moods — he remembers my coffee order — and the greenest flag of all is missing from most lists: the fear of the Lord. "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30), and the same is true of a man. A father tells his daughter: notice the boy who is kind; then ask whether he is kind because he is pleasant or because he belongs to Christ, for the first fades and the second grows. He tells his son: be the green flag before you go looking for one.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (c. 2020–present, opposite of red flag) for a good sign in a person — the slang’s list of virtues, which Scripture calls fruit and crowns with the fear of the Lord.
webster_full: GREEN FLAG, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; opposite of red flag) A trait or habit that signals a person is kind, trustworthy, and worth pursuing as a friend or partner. "He asked my dad first. Green flag."
Posted as a list ("green flags in a girl") or as a green emoji in the comments; green-flag energy, a generally trustworthy manner.
Older senses: the "go" or "all clear" signal on railways; the starting flag in motor racing.

Webster (1828), root word green: “GREEN, adjective 1. Properly, growing, flourishing, as plants; hence, of the color of herbage and plants when growing, a color composed of blue and yellow rays, one of blue and yellow rays, one of the original prismatic colors; verdant. 2. New; fresh; recent; as a green wound. The greenest usurpation. 3. Fresh; flourishing; undecayed;”
Decode for parents: your teen is looking for virtue and calling it a green flag; help him put the fear of the Lord at the top of the list.
scriptures: Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
corruption_summary: Green flag rightly hunts for character, but its list runs to manners and moods and usually leaves off the one mark Scripture puts first, the fear of the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: This is one of the slang’s better instincts. A generation trained by dating apps to sort by photographs is, in the green-flag lists, trying to sort by character: does he keep his word, is she gentle, do they treat the weak well? Scripture commends the question. Samuel was told, "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature" (1Sa 16:7), and the virtues of Galatians 5 are exactly the things a spouse lives with for fifty years.

The trouble is the source of the list. Feed-made green flags are often courtesies a clever unbeliever can perform for months: he remembers your birthday, she likes your friends. Good fruit grows from a good tree (Mat 7:17), and the root of that tree is the fear of the Lord (Pro 31:30). Teach your children to look for the green flags that cannot be faked for long — a man in the Word, a woman at prayer, both under the oversight of a faithful church — and to become them first.
roots_summary: Old English grene (growing, verdant) → railway and racing "go" signal → c. 2020: the opposite of red flag, a good sign in a person.
roots_lines: Old English grene — green, growing, related to grow and grass
19th c. railway signalling: green for "all clear"
20th c. motor racing: the green flag starts the race
c. 2020–2021 TikTok and Twitter: green flag coined against red flag
Now: lists of virtues looked for in a friend or partner
usage: "He apologised to his little sister without anyone making him. Major green flag."
Scripture calls green flags fruit, and lists them (Gal 5:22).
The greenest flag is the fear of the Lord (Pro 31:30).

etymology: A TikTok coinage of early 2023, added to the red-flag / green-flag pair. The first uses described a dating-app match who seemed dull — beige, the colour of nothing in particular — and within weeks the sense shifted to a harmless oddity in a partner, neither good nor bad: he drinks water from only one cup, she narrates what the dog is thinking. The trend invited users to post their partner’s beige flags, and a great many did.
biblical_def: In current slang a beige flag is a quirk: not a warning and not a virtue, just one of those odd, harmless habits that make a person particular. He eats his sandwich in a strict order; she names her houseplants; he thanks the sat-nav. Listing a partner’s beige flags is mostly affectionate. The Christian observation: there is real grace in this word, and it is worth keeping. God made persons, not units, and each of us is "fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14) — down to the particulars. Love learns those particulars and smiles at them. "It is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Pro 19:11); how much more to pass over a quirk that is no transgression at all. Paul asks believers to be "Forbearing one another" (Col 3:13), and "charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1Pe 4:8). A marriage, a family, and a church all run on this kind of good-humoured patience, and "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22). The one caution is the sense the word first carried: do not call a person beige, as if ordinary meant dull. The steady, unremarkable man who keeps his word even when it costs him is the man Psalm 15 says shall never be moved. A father tells his children: learn to tell a beige flag from a red one; laugh at the first, take the second seriously, and never let a quirk become your reason to despise a person God made.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (TikTok, 2023) for a harmless quirk in a person — the small particulars of a fearfully and wonderfully made neighbour, which charity learns to enjoy and forbear.
webster_full: BEIGE FLAG, n. (Gen-Z slang, 2023–present; TikTok) A harmless quirk or odd habit in a person, neither warning nor virtue. "His beige flag is that he names every car he owns."
First sense (early 2023): a sign that a dating match is dull or bland — beige in personality. The quirk sense quickly displaced it.
Older words for the same thing: a foible, an idiosyncrasy, a little way he has. Beige itself is French, the colour of undyed wool.

Webster (1828), root word quirk: “QUIRK, noun quurk. 1. Literally, a turn; a starting from the point or line; hence, an artful turn for evasion or subterfuge; a shift; a quibble; as the quirks of a pettifogger. 2. A fit or turn; a short paroxysm; as a quirk of joy or grief. 3. A smart taunt or retort. I may chance to have some odd quirks and remnants of wit broken on me.”
Decode for parents: one of the gentler trends — teens noticing and enjoying the oddities of people they love.
scriptures: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
corruption_summary: Beige flag is mostly a kindly word for forbearance; its only danger is the sense it began with, that an ordinary person is a dull one.
corruption_paragraphs: Little here needs correcting. To notice that your husband folds his socks in a ritual, and to love him for it, is the forbearance Paul commends (Col 3:13). Families have always kept private jokes about one another’s habits, and the habit of finding them funny rather than infuriating is a grace. "It is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Pro 19:11), and a quirk is not even that.

The caution lies in where the word started: beige as boring, a dating-app verdict on people without enough sparkle. A generation raised on content can begin to treat a quiet, steady person as a defect. Scripture prizes exactly that steadiness: the man who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" (Psa 15:4) is the citizen of God’s holy hill. Teach your children to enjoy the quirks of others, to bear with them cheerfully, and to see that ordinary faithfulness is the least ordinary thing in the world.
roots_summary: French beige (undyed wool colour) + English flag → early 2023 TikTok: a dull dating match → a harmless quirk in a partner.
roots_lines: French beige — the natural colour of undyed wool
English flag — a banner or signal
2020–2021: the red-flag / green-flag pair on TikTok
Early 2023 TikTok: beige flag, at first a sign of blandness
Within weeks: a harmless quirk, posted with affection
usage: "Beige flag: she has to sit on the left side of every booth."
Forbear the quirks; it is charity (Col 3:13).
Fearfully and wonderfully made, down to the oddities (Psa 139:14).

etymology: From counselling vocabulary. Trauma is Greek for a wound; 20th-century psychology extended it to wounds of the mind, and the online therapy culture of the 2010s made it everyday speech. Trauma dumping — unloading painful personal history on someone without warning or invitation — spread on TikTok and Instagram c. 2020–2021, largely through counsellors’ explainer videos during the pandemic lockdowns. It is now used both as a complaint ("she trauma dumped on me at lunch") and as a self-mocking apology ("sorry for the trauma dump").
biblical_def: In current slang to trauma dump is to unload heavy personal history — abuse, grief, a family breaking apart, despair — on someone who did not ask and is not ready for it: a stranger in the comments, a new friend on the first afternoon, a whole following in a video. The phrase is used as a complaint and as an apology. The Christian observation: Scripture does not tell sufferers to be quiet. It commands the opposite: "pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us" (Psa 62:8); "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee" (Psa 55:22). The Psalms are full of men telling God exactly how bad it is. And the church is to carry what the sufferer cannot: "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). What the slang rightly notices is order and fitness. "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Pro 29:11) — not forever, but till the right time and the right ears. A burden laid on a stranger who cannot help, or broadcast to thousands, is not carried; it is scattered. And the hearer has a duty too: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19), not quick to brush off a hurting person with a label. A father tells his children: when the weight is heavy, bring it first to God, then to us, then to your pastor — we are here to carry it with you. And when a friend spills over, do not roll your eyes; sit down, listen, and bring her to people who can help.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (TikTok / Instagram c. 2020–present, from counselling vocabulary) for unloading heavy personal history on an unready listener — a misdirected burden Scripture would pour out first before God and then lay on the shoulders of the church.
webster_full: TRAUMA DUMP, n. / v.i. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; from counselling vocabulary) To unload painful personal history on a listener who did not ask and is unprepared; the act, or the content so unloaded. "Sorry for the trauma dump, I just met you."
Trauma dumping, n., the habit. Used both as a complaint about others and as a self-mocking apology; also of videos that broadcast family pain to strangers.
Older words for the same act: unburdening oneself, pouring one’s heart out, crying on someone’s shoulder — phrases that assumed a friend was there to receive it.

Webster (1828), root word dump: “DUMP, noun […] 1. A dull gloomy state of the mind; sadness; melancholy; sorrow; heaviness of heart. In doleful dumps. 2. Absence of mind; reverie. 3. A melancholy tune or air. […]”
Decode for parents: if your child is pouring out pain to strangers online, the pain is real and the listeners are the wrong ones; make yourself the first ear.
scriptures: Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
corruption_summary: The phrase rightly sees that heavy burdens need fit hearers, but it teaches the hurting to apologise for their sorrow and the hearers to label it rather than carry it.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a real fault the word names. A burden belongs where it can be borne: before God first, then with parents, pastors, and friends who have the standing and the strength to help. Spilled on a classmate in the lunch line or posted for thousands, it lands on people who cannot carry it and are not responsible for it. "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Pro 29:11) — the wise man waits for the right ears; he does not bury the matter forever.

But the label cuts the other way too. A generation that rolls its eyes at an overshare can stop listening altogether, and the hurting learn to open with an apology. Scripture rebukes that coldness: "Bear ye one another’s burdens" (Gal 6:2), "weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). And it offers a Listener who never tires: "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee" (Psa 55:22). Teach your children where to bring their sorrow, and teach them to be the kind of friend another child can bring sorrow to.
roots_summary: Greek trauma (a wound) → 20th-c. psychology: a wound of the mind → 2010s therapy culture → c. 2020 TikTok: trauma dumping, unloading on an unready listener.
roots_lines: Greek trauma — a wound, a hurt
Late 19th–20th c. psychology: wounds of the mind as well as the body
Middle English dumpen — to fall, to throw down; English dump, to unload all at once
2010s online therapy culture: clinical words in everyday speech
c. 2020–2021 TikTok and Instagram: trauma dumping
usage: "She trauma dumped on me in the first ten minutes of chemistry and I didn’t know what to say."
Pour it out before God first; He is a refuge (Psa 62:8).
Then let the church carry it with you (Gal 6:2).

etymology: Coined in 1956 by the sociologists Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl in "Mass Communication and Para-Social Interaction" (Psychiatry), describing the illusion of intimacy television viewers felt with presenters who spoke to the camera as if to a friend. Greek para, beside: a relationship that runs alongside a real one. The academic word went popular in the 2010s and 2020s through YouTube, Twitch, and TikTok, where creators speak daily to followers who feel they know them; Cambridge Dictionary named parasocial its word of the year for 2025.
biblical_def: In current use a parasocial relationship is one-sided: a teen feels she knows a streamer, a singer, or a podcaster as a friend — follows his moods, defends him in the comments, grieves when he quits — while he does not know she exists. Teens use the word of themselves with wry self-awareness: "my parasocial relationship with this YouTuber is getting out of hand." The Christian observation: the word names a real hunger and a real hollowness. We were made to know and be known, and a voice in the earbuds every morning feels like friendship without any of its costs. But Scripture says friendship runs both ways and costs something: "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly" (Pro 18:24). A celebrity cannot do that for you, and you cannot do it for him. "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help" (Psa 146:3); "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm" (Jer 17:5). The remedy is not loneliness but the body of Christ, "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25), where people know your name and your face. And there is one relationship that can look one-sided and is not: the Lord Jesus, whom you have not seen, says, "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine" (Joh 10:14). A father tells his daughter: the people on your screen do not know you; the people at your table and in your pew do, and Christ knows you best of all. Spend your heart where it is known.
webster_summary: From a 1956 sociology coinage, popularized online in the 2010s–2020s, for a one-sided bond with a public figure — a hunger to be known that Scripture answers with the church and with the Shepherd who knows His sheep.
webster_full: PARASOCIAL, adj. (Gen-Z slang usage, 2010s–present; coined 1956) Of a relationship: one-sided, in which a viewer or fan feels close to a public figure who does not know him. "I’m in a parasocial relationship with a guy who reviews sandwiches."
Parasocial relationship, parasocial bond; sometimes shortened to a parasocial. Used self-mockingly, and as a rebuke to fans who act as if they own a celebrity’s private life.
Original sense (Horton and Wohl, 1956): the illusion of face-to-face intimacy created by television presenters who address the camera directly.

Webster (1828), root word stranger: “STRANGER, noun 1. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country. Paris and London are visited by strangers from all the countries of Europe. 2. One of another town, city, state or province in the same country. The Commencements in American colleges are frequented by multitudes of strangers from the neighboring towns and states. 3.”
Decode for parents: the voice your child hears most in a week may belong to someone who will never learn his name.
scriptures: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.
corruption_summary: The parasocial bond offers the feeling of friendship without its duties, and leaves a lonely heart leaning on a stranger instead of on the church and on Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age had its famous men, but no age before ours let a fan hear one talk for three hours a day, in his bedroom, as if to him alone. The feeling of friendship is engineered: the creator looks into the lens, says "you guys," shares his breakfast and his breakups. For a lonely teen it is easier than real friendship, which asks you to show up, be known, and be corrected. Proverbs’ rule, "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly" (Pro 18:24), cannot be kept with a man who does not know you are there.

Scripture’s warning is about where the heart leans: "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm" (Jer 17:5). The answer is a real body — the church, where faces and names are known (Heb 10:25) — and a real Saviour. Christ is the one famous Man who knows every one of His followers: "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep" (Joh 10:14). Help your children trade the screen’s imitation of friendship for the real thing, at home, in the pew, and at the throne of grace.
roots_summary: Greek para (beside) + Latin socius (companion) → 1956 sociology: para-social interaction with television hosts → 2010s–2020s: one-sided bonds with streamers and stars.
roots_lines: Greek para — beside, alongside, near but apart
Latin socius — a companion; English social
1956: Horton and Wohl, para-social interaction with television hosts
2010s YouTube and Twitch: daily creators, devoted audiences
2025: Cambridge Dictionary word of the year
usage: "I was so upset when he stopped posting, and then I remembered he doesn’t know I exist. Parasocial."
Friendship must shew itself friendly; a screen cannot (Pro 18:24).
The Good Shepherd knows His sheep (Joh 10:14).

etymology: French nonchalant, present participle of Old French nonchaloir, not to be concerned, from non + chaloir, to matter, ultimately Latin calere, to be warm. English has used it since the 18th century for calm indifference. On TikTok in 2024–2025 nonchalant became a prized pose, especially among boys: to show no visible excitement, hurt, or effort ("stay nonchalant," "nonchalant king"), with memes mocking anyone who showed eager feeling.
biblical_def: In current slang to be nonchalant is to look unbothered on purpose: no visible excitement when she texts back, no tears at the funeral, no effort that could be laughed at. It is a pose, practised in front of the mirror, and among boys it has become a mark of status: the one who cares least wins. The Christian observation: the word’s own root gives it away. It comes from a Latin word for warm; to be nonchalant is, literally, to be not-warm. Christ’s sharpest words to a church were aimed at exactly that temperature: "thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot" (Rev 3:16). Scripture wants the opposite of a pose: "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11). It wants feeling joined to others: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). And it shows us a Saviour who was never studiedly unbothered. He was moved with compassion, He was zealous for His Father’s house, and at the grave of His friend "Jesus wept" (Joh 11:35). There is a true composure in Scripture — self-control, a quiet spirit, a man who rules his spirit (Pro 16:32) — but it is strength over feeling, not the pretence of having none. A father tells his son: do not be ashamed to care about things that matter. Weep at the grave, sing loud in church, tell the girl’s father you are serious. The pose that cares about nothing is the most anxious pose there is; the man who fears God can afford to be warm.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (TikTok 2024–present, from French nonchalant, literally not-warm) for a studied pose of unbothered indifference — the lukewarmness Christ rebukes, set against the warm and ruled heart of a man who fears God.
webster_full: NONCHALANT, adj. (Gen-Z slang usage, c. 2024–present; from French) Deliberately unbothered; showing no visible eagerness, hurt, or effort, as a pose that earns status. "She left him on read and he stayed nonchalant."
Being nonchalant, staying nonchalant; nonchalant king, a boy admired for his indifference. The opposite, mocked: being eager, emotional, or visibly invested.
Standard English since the 18th century: calm, casually unconcerned — the sense a grandparent knows, without the pose.

Webster (1828), root word cool: “COOL, adjective […] 1. Moderately cold; being of a temperature between hot and cold; as cool air; cool water. 2. Not ardent or zealous; not angry; not fond; not excited by passion of any kind; indifferent; as a cool friend; a cool temper; a cool lover. 3. Not retaining heat; light; as a cool dress.”
Decode for parents: your son may be learning that showing he cares is losing; he needs to see a man who is strong and warm at once.
scriptures: I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
corruption_summary: Nonchalant makes a virtue of seeming not to care, teaching boys a lukewarm pose in place of the ruled but fervent heart Scripture commends.
corruption_paragraphs: The pose is a defence. If you never show that you want anything, no one can mock you for not getting it; if you never weep, no one can see where you are hurt. Teens are not wrong to fear mockery, but nonchalance is costly armour. It shuts out the joy of eager love, the honest grief of loss, and the zeal that serves God "fervent in spirit" (Rom 12:11). Christ’s word to Laodicea, "I would thou wert cold or hot" (Rev 3:15), is a judgment on spiritual temperature, and the nonchalant soul is drilling itself in the wrong one.

Scripture does commend composure: "he that ruleth his spirit" is better "than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). But ruling a spirit means there is a spirit to rule. The Lord Jesus slept in the storm and wept at a grave (Joh 11:35); He was never cool toward His Father or His friends. Show your children that pattern. A man secure in God can risk being seen to care, because his worth does not hang on the room’s reaction.
roots_summary: Latin calere (to be warm) → Old French nonchaloir (not to be concerned) → 18th-c. English nonchalant, calmly unconcerned → 2024 TikTok: a prized pose of not caring.
roots_lines: Latin calere — to be warm
Old French chaloir — to matter, to concern; nonchaloir, not to care
18th c. English nonchalant — casually unconcerned
20th c. cool: the jazz-age pose of calm detachment
2024–2025 TikTok: stay nonchalant, indifference as status
usage: "I wanted to celebrate but I had to stay nonchalant in front of everybody."
Not-warm is the old name for lukewarm (Rev 3:16).
Jesus wept, and was no less a man for it (Joh 11:35).

etymology: From a drawing by the artist Phillip Banks, posted in October 2023, of a cartoon dog in a grey sweater, rolled-up jeans, and red sneakers, hands in pockets, with a faint smirk. In November 2024 it exploded on TikTok and X as the "chill guy" meme, in videos captioned with variations of "just a chill guy who lowkey doesn’t care" (the original caption used a crude acronym) set over stressful situations the chill guy shrugs off. Chill for relaxed is older American slang: chill out (c. 1979, spread by 1980s hip-hop), and the adjective chill, easygoing, in the 1990s.
biblical_def: In current slang the chill guy is the meme of easy composure: a cartoon dog with his hands in his pockets, unbothered while the exam is failing, the car is towed, or the group project collapses. Teens post themselves as the chill guy to laugh at their own stress, and "he’s a chill guy" is high praise among boys. The Christian observation: there is a composure Scripture loves and one it rebukes, and the meme mixes them. The good one is real: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Php 4:6), and "the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus" (Php 4:7). "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee" (Isa 26:3). The calmest man in the Gospels is the Lord Jesus "in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow" while His disciples panicked (Mar 4:38) — and when He woke He did not shrug; He rebuked the wind. His calm came from trusting His Father, not from not caring. The bad composure is the sluggard’s: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep" (Pro 6:10). Hands in pockets while the work goes undone is not peace; it is the road to want. A father tells his son: be calm in a crisis and never careless about your duty. Pray, then work. The calm that comes from trusting God takes the hands out of the pockets.
webster_summary: Gen-Z meme (Phillip Banks drawing, 2023; viral November 2024) of easy, hands-in-pockets composure — a calm Scripture commends when it rests on trusting God and rebukes when it is the sluggard’s shrug.
webster_full: CHILL GUY, n. phr. (Gen-Z slang, 2024–present; internet meme) One who stays relaxed and unbothered under pressure; from the "just a chill guy" cartoon dog. "Phone at two percent, no charger, I’m a chill guy."
Used of oneself in self-mockery during stress, and of others as praise: "He’s a chill guy," easygoing, low-drama. The image itself is posted as a reaction.
Older slang: chill, chill out (1980s–90s), relax; a chill person, easy company. Before that, chill meant cold, and a chill the shiver before a fever.

Webster (1828), root word chill: “CHILL, noun 1. A shivering with cold; rigors, as in an ague; the cold fit that precedes a fever; sensation of cold in an animal body; chilliness. […] 2. A moderate degree of cold; chilliness in any body; that which gives the sensation of cold.”
Decode for parents: when your son says he is a chill guy about the test, he may be joking about his nerves or announcing that he has stopped studying; ask which.
scriptures: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep:
corruption_summary: The chill guy meme blurs the peace of a man who trusts God with the shrug of a man who has stopped caring, and the hands in its pockets belong to the second.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of the meme is harmless self-mockery — a stressed teenager laughing at himself — and there is a real virtue near it. Scripture forbids fretting: "Be careful for nothing" (Php 4:6). It promises peace to the mind stayed on God (Isa 26:3). A boy who can keep his head when the bus breaks down is learning something good, and "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty" (Pro 16:32).

But the chill guy’s calm has no source. He is unbothered because he has decided not to be bothered, and his hands stay in his pockets. That is the posture Proverbs warns against: "a little folding of the hands to sleep" ends in want that comes "as an armed man" (Pro 6:10–11). Christ’s calm in the storm was the calm of a Son resting in His Father, and it rose up to act. Teach your children the difference: peace that prays and then works, not indifference that shrugs and then drifts.
roots_summary: Old English ciele (cold) → chill, coldness → c. 1980 chill out, relax → 2023 drawing, 2024 meme: just a chill guy.
roots_lines: Old English ciele — cold, coolness
Middle English chill — a shiver; to make cold
c. 1979–1980s American slang: chill out, calm down
1990s: chill, adj., relaxed, easygoing
October 2023 drawing by Phillip Banks; November 2024 viral meme: just a chill guy
usage: "Lost my phone, missed the bus, test in five minutes. I’m just a chill guy."
Calm that prays: the peace of God keeps the heart (Php 4:7).
Calm that shrugs: folded hands end in want (Pro 6:10).

etymology: English girl with the affectionate diminutive -ie, in use since the 19th century, especially in Scots and in the mouths of fathers and grandmothers ("come here, girlie"). Gen Z revived it on TikTok c. 2021–2022, borrowing the bright, warm tone of pop-fandom speech: girlie as cheerful address between young women ("hi girlie!"), and the girlies for women or fans as a group ("the girlies are obsessed with this song").
biblical_def: In current slang girlie is a warm, breezy word for a young woman: a greeting ("hey girlie"), a cheer ("go off, girlie"), or a collective noun ("the girlies" at a concert, "girlies who read"). It signals friendliness and a shared, light-hearted femininity. The Christian observation: there is nothing wrong with tender words for girls; the Bible has its own. When the Lord Jesus raised Jairus’ daughter, He "took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise" (Mar 5:41) — and talitha is an Aramaic word of fondness, little girl. Paul tells Timothy to treat "the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2). The psalmist prays "that our daughters may be as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace" (Psa 144:12) — girlhood as something weight-bearing and beautiful. What the slang lacks is that weight. The girlies are often a market — for skincare, concert tours, and a girlishness meant to last forever — and Scripture wants girls to grow into women whose adorning is "the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4) and who fear the Lord (Pro 31:30). A father tells his daughter: you can be warm, light-hearted, and girlish, and you are also being built into a corner stone. Let your friends call you girlie; let the Lord call you His.
webster_summary: Gen-Z revival (TikTok c. 2021–present) of the old diminutive girlie, a cheerful address for a young woman — a tenderness Christ Himself used, meant to grow into a woman’s strength.
webster_full: GIRLIE, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; revived diminutive) A warm, casual address for a young woman or girl; plural the girlies, young women as a group. "Hi girlie, love your jacket!"
Also spelled girly; extended to girly pop. The girlies for a fan base or a crowd ("the girlies who journal"). Used chiefly among young women, and by older women to younger ones.
Older senses: a fond diminutive for a little girl, from a parent or grandparent; as an adjective, girlish, sometimes in a slighting tone.
Webster (1828), root word girl: “GIRL, noun gerl. […] 1. A female child, or young woman. In familiar language, any young unmarried woman. 2. Among sportsmen, a roebuck of two years old.”
Decode for parents: mostly harmless warmth; listen for whether "the girlies" means your daughter’s friends or a market selling to her.
scriptures: And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; that our daughters may be as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace:
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
corruption_summary: Girlie is a kindly word that can stay kindly, but the slang tends to freeze girls in girlhood and sell to them as the girlies, where Scripture builds daughters into corner stones.
corruption_paragraphs: Little in the word itself needs rebuke. Tender names for girls are as old as fathers, and the Lord Jesus used one at a deathbed (Mar 5:41). Friends who greet each other with warmth are doing something good, and Paul’s rule for how young men are to regard young women, "as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2), is a better frame than most of the culture offers.

The danger is in the plural and the marketing. The girlies is how brands and tours speak to young women, and the girlhood they sell has no end: skincare at ten, a cartoon femininity at thirty, adulthood indefinitely deferred. Scripture’s picture is growth. Daughters are to become "corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace" (Psa 144:12) — bearing weight, beautiful because useful — and their adorning is to be "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). Keep the warmth; aim it toward womanhood.
roots_summary: Middle English girle (a child) → girl, a young female → 19th-c. diminutive girlie → c. 2021 TikTok: hi girlie, the girlies.
roots_lines: Middle English gurle, girle — a child of either sex, origin uncertain
16th c.: girl narrowed to a young female
19th c.: girlie, fond diminutive, especially in Scots
c. 2021–2022 TikTok: girlie as greeting; the girlies as a crowd
Related forms: girly pop, it girl
usage: "Okay girlie, we are going to the library and we are not leaving till this essay is done."
Christ spoke tenderly to a little girl and raised her up (Mar 5:41).
Daughters are built as corner stones (Psa 144:12).

etymology: A playful extension of girly / girlie with pop (as in pop star, and a bright, bubbly sound), current on stan Twitter and TikTok c. 2021–2022. It belongs to a camp register — exaggerated, theatrical, tongue-in-cheek — and is used as fond address ("thank you, girly pop") or as gently ironic description of someone very bubbly and feminine. Also spelled girlypop.
biblical_def: In current slang girly pop is an exaggerated, cheerful address for a young woman, said with a wink: "yes, girly pop," "okay, girly pop, calm down." Sometimes it is pure affection, sometimes gentle teasing of someone very bubbly, and sometimes it is quietly patronising. The register is camp: big, theatrical, never quite serious. The Christian observation: Scripture has room for delight and play. There is "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4), and the godly woman of Proverbs "shall rejoice in time to come" (Pro 31:25). Girls being light-hearted and cheering one another on is no sin. But camp is a register that never commits, and it can teach a girl to speak of herself and her friends as a performance — all sparkle, nothing serious. Paul warns against "foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks" (Eph 5:4) — not against laughter, but against speech with nothing under it. The woman Scripture praises is glad because she is strong: "Strength and honour are her clothing" (Pro 31:25), and "a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30). Her adorning is not costly array but "good works" (1Ti 2:10). A father tells his daughter: be bright and glad and full of laughter, and be more than bubbly. When your friends call you girly pop, let them also find in you someone they can bring a serious thing to.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (stan Twitter / TikTok c. 2021–present) for a camp, cheerful address to a young woman — a playfulness Scripture allows, so long as there is strength and honour under the sparkle.
webster_full: GIRLY POP, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; camp register) A playful, exaggerated address for a young woman, or a description of one who is very bubbly and feminine. "You got the job? Yes, girly pop!"
Also girlypop. Affectionate, teasing, or condescending depending on tone ("okay, girly pop").
Built from girly (girlish) and pop (pop music, and a bright bubbly sound); older cousins in a grandmother’s kitchen: sweetie, doll, sugar.
Webster (1828), root word pop: “POP, noun A small smart quick sound or report.”
Decode for parents: usually friendly fun; listen for whether it is said with warmth or with a sneer.
scriptures: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
corruption_summary: Girly pop is mostly harmless play, but its camp register trains girls to perform femininity as sparkle and irony rather than to wear strength and honour.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to rebuke in a friend cheering "yes, girly pop!" when another gets good news. Scripture gives laughter and dancing their time (Ecc 3:4), and "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22). The word’s cousins — doll, sweetie — have been in kitchens and offices for a century, and most of the time this one is just as kind.

The caution is in the register. Camp is speech that is always half-joking, theatrical, and safely unserious; it came to the word through fandom culture, where everything is performance. A girl who learns to speak only in that key can find it hard to speak plainly about anything that matters. Paul’s warning about "foolish talking" (Eph 5:4) is a warning about speech with nothing under it. Proverbs 31 sets the pattern: a woman who "shall rejoice in time to come" because "Strength and honour are her clothing" (Pro 31:25). Let the laughter stay; build the strength under it.
roots_summary: Girl → girly (girlish) + pop (bright, bubbly; pop music) → c. 2021 stan Twitter and TikTok: girly pop, camp address.
roots_lines: Middle English girle → girly, girlish
Imitative English pop — a small, sharp, bright sound
20th c.: pop music, short for popular
c. 2021–2022 stan Twitter and TikTok: girly pop
Now: fond, teasing, or ironic address
usage: "Okay girly pop, you passed your driving test, we are getting ice cream."
A time to laugh, and a time to dance (Ecc 3:4).
Strength and honour under the sparkle (Pro 31:25).

etymology: A clipping of sister, used in American English as a family nickname since at least the mid-19th century. In African-American Vernacular English sis has long been a warm address for a female friend or fellow woman, and from Black Twitter c. 2016–2018 it spread across the internet in reaction phrases ("sis, no," "okay, sis," "sis is thriving"), often in the third person for a woman being cheered or gently teased.
biblical_def: In current slang sis is how a girl addresses a friend who is not her sister — "sis, you look amazing," "sis, that is a bad idea" — and how commenters speak of a woman they are rooting for or roasting: "sis really thought she did something." It carries closeness, loyalty, and sometimes a scolding tone only family can use. The Christian observation: this is a word the church had first. Christ looked at those around Him and said, "whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Mat 12:50). Paul commends "Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church" (Rom 16:1), and charges Timothy to treat "the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2). James makes sisterhood practical: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food" (Jas 2:15), warm words are not enough. Even wisdom is to be called by the name: "Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister" (Pro 7:4). The slang’s sis is a kindness, but it is shallow: a sisterhood of moods, quick to be offered and quick to be withdrawn. In Christ it is blood-deep — the blood of the Lamb — and it binds women who would never have chosen one another. A father tells his daughter: call your friends sis if you like; then be one, the way the church means it — loyal, pure, practical, and bound together under the same Father in heaven.
webster_summary: Clipped sister (19th-c. American; AAVE address; Black Twitter c. 2016–present) as warm address for a female friend — a closeness Christ deepened into the sisterhood of all who do His Father’s will.
webster_full: SIS, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2016–present; AAVE origin) A familiar address for a female friend or fellow woman; also used in the third person of a woman being cheered or teased. "Sis, you did not just text him back."
Reaction phrases: "okay sis," "sis, no," "sis is thriving." Sister is used in the same warm address; bestie is its close cousin.
Older sense: a family nickname for one’s own sister or a little girl, in American homes since the 19th century — "Sis" at the dinner table.

Webster (1828), root word sister: “SIS'TER, noun 1. A female born of the same patents; correlative to brother. 2. A woman of the same faith; a female fellow christian. If a brother or sister be naked and destitute of daily food. James 2:15. 3. A female of the same kind. 4. One of the same kind, or of the same condition; as sister-fruits. 5. A female of the same society;”
Decode for parents: a friendly word; the question is whether your daughter’s friends are sisters in the slang’s sense or in the church’s.
scriptures: For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food,
Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman:
corruption_summary: Sis borrows the language of family for friendship, a good instinct that the slang leaves shallow and that the church fills with blood-bought, practical sisterhood.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is a kindness. It says, you are mine to cheer for and mine to correct; it gives a friend the standing of family. Scripture approves the instinct: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17), and the same is true of a sister. In the comments, though, sis is tossed at strangers and used as easily to mock as to bless, and the family it names lasts about as long as the scroll.

The church has the real thing. Christ named His sisters by obedience, not by blood (Mat 12:50); Paul entrusted Phebe with his letter to Rome (Rom 16:1); James tied sisterhood to bread and clothing (Jas 2:15). Teach your daughter to call her friends sis and mean it in that sense: to pray for them, to tell them the truth, to show up when they are in need, and to look for sisters in the pew who are older and wiser than she is.
roots_summary: Old English sweostor / Old Norse systir → sister → 19th-c. American sis → AAVE address → c. 2016 Black Twitter: sis for any female friend.

usage: "Sis, you’ve been crying over him for a week. We’re going for a walk."
Whoever does the Father’s will is Christ’s sister (Mat 12:50).
Treat the younger as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2).
